title: Perseus. Atlas. Andromeda
titleEn: Atlas Turned to Stone, and Andromeda Freed — Metamorphoses IV.604–752
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Perseus is in flight with Medusa's severed head: he crosses Libya (where the blood dripping from it breeds the snakes of that country), is blown about the world by quarrelling winds, and comes down at nightfall in the western kingdom of Atlas. Refused hospitality by that huge son of the Titan Iapetus, who has been warned by an oracle that a son of Jupiter will one day strip his golden tree, he shows him Medusa's face, and Atlas becomes the mountain on which the sky rests. Flying on, he finds Andromeda chained to a rock on the Ethiopian shore, given up on the order of the oracle of Ammon because her mother Cassiope boasted of her beauty; he bargains with her parents for her hand, kills the sea-monster, and frees her. The part opens by looking back at Cadmus and Harmonia, just turned to serpents, and at Acrisius of Argos, who denied both the god Bacchus and his own grandson Perseus; it closes with the making of the first coral.

advisory.lede: This part refers twice to Jupiter's rape of Danae, Perseus' mother: a god impregnating a woman shut away in a locked chamber by her own father.
advisory.more: Ovid gives it in half a line each time. At 611 Perseus is the child 'whom Danae conceived by a rain of gold'; at 697-698 Perseus himself, asking Cepheus and Cassiope for the chained Andromeda, names his mother as the woman 'whom, shut away, Jupiter filled with fruitful gold'. Nothing in the Latin gives Danae a voice, a choice or a refusal; the grammar makes her the object of the verb both times, and her confinement, imposed by her father Acrisius to prevent the birth, is part of what the god comes through. The text is presented unaltered and the translation does not soften either passage: the boast is Perseus' own, and it is made in front of the woman he is bargaining for.

sentences.t:
Sed tamen ambobus versae solacia formae
magna nepos dederat, quem debellata colebat
India, quem positis celebrabat Achaia templis.
sentences.l: But even so, for their changed shape consolations, and great ones, their grandson had given to them both, whom conquered India worshipped, whom Achaia honoured with temples set up.
sentences.i: Yet their grandson had given them both great consolation for their changed shape, he whom India, beaten in war, worshipped, whom Achaea honoured with temples raised to him.
sentences.n: The 'both' are Cadmus and Harmonia, who have just been turned into serpents; the grandson is Bacchus, son of their daughter Semele, who conquered India and was given cult in Greece. 'positis ... templis' is an ablative absolute, literally 'temples having been set up', where English wants a clause: this construction is everywhere in Latin verse and worth learning to hear as a clause. Note how 'solacia' is split from its adjective 'magna' across the line-break, a habit of the hexameter.

sentences.t:
Solus Abantiades ab origine cretus eadem
Acrisius superest, qui moenibus arceat urbis
Argolicae contraque deum ferat arma genusque
non putet esse Iovis;
sentences.l: Alone the son of Abas, sprung from the same origin, Acrisius, remains: one to shut [the god] out from the walls of the Argive city, and to bear arms against him, and not to think that his line is Jupiter's;
sentences.i: Only Acrisius, of the line of Abas, sprung from that same stock, holds out: a man to bar the god from the walls of Argos, to take up arms against him, and to deny that the god's line comes from Jupiter;
sentences.n: 'Abantiades' means 'descendant of Abas' - a patronymic used in place of a name, standard Ovidian shorthand, and the same name will be used of Perseus at 673, since Perseus is Acrisius' grandson. 'ab origine cretus eadem' means sprung from the same stock as the god he is resisting: both houses run back through Belus to Io and her father the river Inachus - which is also why Perseus is called 'Inachides' at 720. The three verbs arceat, ferat and putet are subjunctive: a relative clause of characteristic, 'the sort of man who would...', not a plain record of what he did. 'arceat' has no expressed object; '[the god]', Bacchus, is supplied here, and the 'genus' of the third clause is the god's line as well: 'X esse Iovis', 'X is Jupiter's', is the very construction that returns at 610-611 of Perseus.

sentences.t:
neque enim Iovis esse putabat
Persea, quem pluvio Danae conceperat auro.
sentences.l: for he did not think that Perseus was Jupiter's, whom Danae had conceived by a rain of gold.
sentences.i: For he would not believe Perseus was Jupiter's son either, Perseus whom Danae conceived by a shower of gold.
sentences.n: 'Iovis esse' is a genitive of possession inside indirect statement: 'to be of Jupiter', that is, to be his son. Danae was Acrisius' own daughter, shut in a chamber because an oracle told him her son would kill him; the god came in as falling gold. Ovid compresses the whole thing into a two-word ablative, 'pluvio ... auro' - see this part's advisory.

sentences.t:
Mox tamen Acrisium (tanta est praesentia veri)
tam violasse deum quam non agnosse nepotem
paenitet:
sentences.l: Soon, though, it repents Acrisius - so great is the presence of truth - as much of having outraged the god as of not having acknowledged his grandson:
sentences.i: Soon, though, Acrisius came to regret - so strong is the force of plain truth - both his outrage against the god and his refusal to own his grandson:
sentences.n: 'paenitet' is impersonal: the person who repents stands in the accusative (Acrisium) and the thing repented of in infinitives (violasse, agnosse, syncopated for violavisse and agnovisse). 'tanta est praesentia veri' is a sententia, a one-line general truth dropped into the story: the truth is present, standing there, and forces itself on a man. The balanced 'tam ... quam' weighs the two offences as equal.

sentences.t:
inpositus iam caelo est alter, at alter
viperei referens spolium memorabile monstri
aera carpebat tenerum stridentibus alis.
sentences.l: the one has now been set in the sky, but the other, carrying back the memorable spoil of the snaky monster, was plucking at the thin air with whirring wings.
sentences.i: The one is already set in heaven; the other, bringing back the famous trophy of the snake-haired monster, was cutting the thin air on hissing wings.
sentences.n: 'alter ... alter' is 'the one ... the other': Bacchus, now a god in heaven, and Perseus, still in mid-flight. The 'spoil of the snaky monster' is Medusa's severed head, 'viperei' pointing at the snakes she has for hair. 'aera carpebat' is 'plucked at the air', the verb used of a traveller eating up a road; the imperfect keeps Perseus in motion while the perfect 'inpositus est' disposes of Bacchus in a word. The edition prints 'inp-' where later texts print 'imp-', and we keep it.

sentences.t:
Cumque super Libycas victor penderet harenas,
Gorgonei capitis guttae cecidere cruentae.
sentences.l: And when, victorious, he was hanging above the Libyan sands, bloody drops fell from the Gorgon's head.
sentences.n: 'cecidere' is 'ceciderunt': the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere, extremely common in hexameter and often the first thing that makes a line look strange. You will meet it again at 729 (maduere) and 736 (inplevere). 'penderet' is the verb for a bird holding still on the air, not for hanging from something.

sentences.t:
Quas humus exceptas varios animavit in angues:
unde frequens illa est infestaque terra colubris.
sentences.l: Which the ground, having caught them, brought to life into snakes of many kinds: from which that land is thick with serpents and dangerous with them.
sentences.i: The ground caught them and quickened them into snakes of every kind; that is why that country teems with serpents and is deadly with them.
sentences.n: 'Quas' opens the sentence: a connecting relative, which English turns into 'and these' or simply starts afresh. Latin uses it constantly to stitch one sentence to the last, and spotting it saves a lot of confusion. 'exceptas' agrees with 'quas' and packs a whole clause into one word, 'having caught them'. This is an aetiology, a story told to explain why something in the world is as it is - here the snakes of Libya - and the poem is built of them.

sentences.t:
Inde per inmensum ventis discordibus actus
nunc huc, nunc illuc exemplo nubis aquosae
fertur et ex alto seductas aethere longe
despectat terras totumque supervolat orbem.
sentences.l: From there, driven through the immeasurable by warring winds, now this way, now that, after the manner of a watery cloud he is carried, and from the high upper air looks down on lands drawn far away below, and flies over the whole world.
sentences.i: From there the quarrelling winds drove him across the immensity, now this way, now that, like a raincloud; he is swept along, looks down from the high air on lands set far beneath him, and flies over the whole globe.
sentences.n: 'per inmensum' is a neuter adjective used as a noun, 'through the immeasurable [space]' - Latin does this freely where English needs a noun. 'exemplo nubis aquosae' is an ablative of manner, 'on the model of a watery cloud'. Watch the tenses: 'fertur' and 'despectat' are present although the narrative around them is past. This is the historic present, which pulls the flight into the reader's own moment, and Ovid switches in and out of it constantly to speed and slow the story.

sentences.t:
Ter gelidas Arctos, ter Cancri bracchia vidit:
saepe sub occasus, saepe est ablatus in ortus.
sentences.l: Three times he saw the icy Bears, three times the arms of the Crab; often he was carried off towards the settings, often into the risings.
sentences.i: Three times he saw the frozen Bears, three times the claws of the Crab; again and again he was swept off towards the sunset, again towards the sunrise.
sentences.n: The Bears (Ursa Major and Minor) stand for the frozen far north; the Crab (Cancer) is the sign in which the sun turns at midsummer and which gives the northern tropic its name, so the pair measures the sky from pole to burning zone, while the settings and risings of the next line measure it from west to east. 'bracchia' are the constellation's claws, literally its 'arms'. 'occasus' and 'ortus' are plural nouns for the sun's settings and risings, used as compass points.

sentences.t:
Iamque cadente die, veritus se credere nocti,
constitit Hesperio, regnis Atlantis, in orbe,
exiguamque petit requiem, dum Lucifer ignes
evocet Aurorae, currus Aurora diurnos.
sentences.l: And now, with the day falling, having feared to entrust himself to the night, he halted in the Hesperian region, the realm of Atlas, and sought a scant rest, until the Morning Star should call out the fires of Dawn, and Dawn the chariot of the day.
sentences.i: And now, as the day sank, afraid to trust himself to the night, he came to rest in the western land, the realm of Atlas, and looked for a little sleep, until the Morning Star should summon the fires of Dawn, and Dawn the chariot of day.
sentences.n: 'cadente die' is another ablative absolute, 'with the day going down'. 'dum' with the subjunctive (evocet) means 'until such time as', with a shade of purpose: he waits for the dawn rather than merely until it. The last clause has no verb of its own - 'currus Aurora diurnos [evocet]' borrows the verb from the line above - a compression Latin allows and English cannot. 'Hesperio ... in orbe' is the west, where Atlas' kingdom lies at the world's edge.

sentences.t:
Hic hominum cunctis ingenti corpore praestans
Iapetionides Atlas fuit.
sentences.l: Here, outdoing all men in his huge body, Atlas the son of Iapetus was.
sentences.i: Here was Atlas, son of Iapetus, a man of a bulk beyond any other's.
sentences.n: 'Iapetionides' is a Greek patronymic, 'son of Iapetus', one of the Titans; Ovid likes these long sonorous forms and uses them where prose would use a name. 'praestans' takes a dative of the people surpassed (cunctis) and an ablative of respect (ingenti corpore): 'standing out to all men in respect of his huge body'. The name is held back to the end of the sentence, after the whole account of his size, so the reader meets the bulk before the man.

sentences.t:
Ultima tellus
rege sub hoc et pontus erat, qui Solis anhelis
aequora subdit equis et fessos excipit axes.
sentences.l: Under this king lay the farthest land, and the sea which puts its waters beneath the Sun's panting horses and takes in his weary axle.
sentences.i: Under his rule lay the world's last land, and the sea that spreads its waters beneath the Sun's panting horses and receives his weary chariot.
sentences.n: The far west was the edge of the world, where the sun goes down into the ocean, and the 'panting horses' are the sun-team at the end of the day's run. 'axes', the axle, stands for the whole chariot: a part named for the whole, a habit of this poem. Note 'rege sub hoc', with the preposition wedged between adjective and noun - normal in verse and worth expecting rather than puzzling over.

sentences.t:
Mille greges illi totidemque armenta per herbas
errabant, et humum vicinia nulla premebant.
sentences.l: A thousand flocks for him, and as many herds, wandered through the grass, and no neighbouring [beasts] pressed the ground.
sentences.i: A thousand flocks were his, and as many herds, straying over the grass, and no neighbour's animals trod that soil.
sentences.n: 'illi' is a dative of possession, 'to him were a thousand flocks': the ordinary Latin way of saying he owned them. 'greges' are sheep and goats, 'armenta' cattle and horses, so the pair means livestock of every kind. The last clause is compressed to the point of obscurity: 'vicinia nulla' is 'no neighbouring [herd]', and the sense is that nobody else's animals ever set foot on his ground. Magnus prints the plural 'premebant', which needs that unexpressed plural subject; some editions print the singular 'premebat', which makes 'vicinia', the neighbourhood itself, the subject - 'no neighbouring land pressed on his soil'. The boast comes out much the same; the grammar does not.

sentences.t:
Arboreae frondes auro radiante nitentes
ex auro ramos, ex auro poma tegebant.
sentences.l: Tree-leaves, shining with radiant gold, covered branches of gold, fruit of gold.
sentences.i: Leaves gleaming with radiant gold covered branches of gold and fruit of gold.
sentences.n: This is the garden of the Hesperides at the western edge of the world, whose golden apples became Hercules' eleventh labour. The repetition is deliberate: the gold is named three times across the two lines, once for the leaves, once for the branches, once for the fruit, with 'ex auro ... ex auro' falling twice in the second. 'poma' is any tree-fruit, not specifically the apple that English has settled on.

sentences.t:
“Hospes,” ait Perseus illi, “seu gloria tangit
te generis magni, generis mihi Iuppiter auctor;
sentences.l: 'Host,' Perseus says to him, 'if the glory of a great line touches you - of my line Jupiter is the founder;
sentences.i: 'Host,' Perseus said to him, 'if the glory of great descent moves you - my line was founded by Jupiter;
sentences.n: 'hospes' covers both guest and host: one word for both sides of the sacred guest-friendship Perseus is invoking, and English has no single equivalent. 'seu ... sive' (here and at 641) sets up 'whether ... or': he offers Atlas two separate reasons to take him in. 'generis' is carried over the line-break and picked up by repetition, the sort of hinge on which Ovid builds long sentences.

sentences.t:
sive es mirator rerum, mirabere nostras.
Hospitium requiemque peto.”
sentences.l: or if you are an admirer of deeds, you will admire ours. I seek hospitality and rest.'
sentences.i: or if great deeds are what you admire, you will admire mine. I ask for shelter and rest.'
sentences.n: 'mirator ... mirabere', noun and verb from one root set side by side: Latin enjoys the figure, and here it does real work, since Perseus is boasting in the act of asking a favour. 'mirabere' is the alternative second-person singular future ending -bere for -beris, standard in verse. 'nostras' is a plural used for 'my', in this mouth as much self-importance as modesty.

sentences.t:
Memor ille vetustae
sortis erat: Themis hanc dederat Parnasia sortem:
sentences.l: He was mindful of an ancient oracle: Themis of Parnassus had given this oracle:
sentences.i: But he remembered an old prophecy - Themis of Parnassus had given it:
sentences.n: 'memor' takes the genitive of the thing remembered ('sortis'). A 'sors' is a lot drawn, and so an oracular answer, since oracles were commonly given by lot; the word is repeated in the next breath as 'sortem'. Themis is the Titaness of settled order and held the oracle at Delphi, which lies under Parnassus, before Apollo took the shrine over.

sentences.t:
“Tempus, Atla, veniet, tua quo spoliabitur auro
arbor, et hunc praedae titulum Iove natus habebit.”
sentences.l: 'A time will come, Atlas, in which your tree will be stripped of its gold, and one born of Jupiter will have the credit of this plunder.'
sentences.i: 'A time will come, Atlas, when your tree will be stripped of its gold, and the glory of that spoil will go to a son of Jupiter.'
sentences.n: 'quo' ('in which') belongs to 'Tempus', the first word of the sentence, but sits deep inside its own clause, with 'tua' in front of it and its verb and noun ('spoliabitur ... arbor') strung out after it across the line-break: finding the relative and then hunting back for its antecedent is half of reading Latin verse. 'Iove natus' is 'born from Jupiter', an ablative of origin. The oracle is true and Atlas misreads it: the son of Jupiter who will take the apples is Hercules, generations later, not the man standing in front of him.

sentences.t:
Id metuens solidis pomaria clauserat Atlas
moenibus et vasto dederat servanda draconi
arcebatque suis externos finibus omnes.
sentences.l: Fearing that, Atlas had closed his orchards with solid walls and had given them to a huge dragon to be guarded, and kept all strangers away from his borders.
sentences.n: 'servanda' is a gerundive, the verbal adjective of obligation, 'to be guarded'; 'dare servanda' is the standard idiom for handing something over for someone else to look after. The two pluperfects (clauserat, dederat) set up a standing arrangement, and then the imperfect (arcebat) makes the barring habitual: this is what he always did. The dragon is Ladon, coiled round the golden tree.

sentences.t:
Huic quoque “vade procul, ne longe gloria rerum,
quam mentiris” ait, “longe tibi Iuppiter absit!”
sentences.l: To this man too he says, 'Go far off, lest the glory of deeds, which you lie about, be far from you, and Jupiter far from you!'
sentences.i: To him too he said: 'Be off with you, or you may find that the glory you lie about, and your Jupiter with it, are a long way off when you want them.'
sentences.n: 'quoque' here is the plain adverb 'too', but be warned: the same shape is often 'quo-que', 'and with which', and telling the two apart is a running task in this poem. The threat is sarcastic - 'may they be far from you' means 'they will be no use to you'. 'mentiris' calls Perseus' descent and his deeds an outright lie: the contempt is Atlas' own, not the poem's, and the reader has just been told that both are true.

sentences.t:
vimque minis addit manibusque expellere temptat
cunctantem et placidis miscentem fortia dictis.
sentences.l: and he adds force to his threats, and tries to drive out with his hands the man hesitating and mixing brave words with peaceable ones.
sentences.i: and he backed his threats with force, trying to drive him out by hand as he lingered, mixing firm words with mild ones.
sentences.n: 'cunctantem' and 'miscentem' are participles used as nouns, 'the one hesitating', 'the one mixing', and together they are the object of 'expellere'; Latin can leave the person unnamed like this where English must supply 'him'. 'placidis ... dictis' is an ablative with 'miscentem': he is folding hard words into soft ones, still trying to keep the exchange civil while being manhandled.

sentences.t:
Viribus inferior (quis enim par esset Atlantis
viribus?) “at quoniam parvi tibi gratia nostra est,
accipe munus!” ait,
sentences.l: The lesser in strength - for who would be a match for the strength of Atlas? - 'but since my thanks are of little [worth] to you, take a gift!' he says,
sentences.i: The weaker in strength - for who could match the strength of Atlas? - he said: 'But since my thanks count for so little with you, take a gift instead!'
sentences.n: 'parvi' is a genitive of value, 'at a small [price]', that is, 'you rate my thanks cheap'; Latin prices things in the genitive and the idiom is worth knowing on sight. 'esset' is subjunctive because the question is rhetorical, 'who would be'. 'accipe munus' is grim irony: the gift is Medusa's face, and the word for it is the ordinary word for a guest-gift, which is exactly what Atlas has refused to give.

sentences.t:
laevaque a parte Medusae
ipse retro versus squalentia protulit ora.
sentences.l: and from the left side, himself turned backwards, he held out the filthy face of Medusa.
sentences.i: and, from his left, himself turned away, he thrust out Medusa's foul head.
sentences.n: 'retro versus' is 'turned back': Perseus himself must not look at what he is holding out, and that turning away is the whole mechanics of using the head. 'squalentia' means rough, matted, filthy, and is used both of scales and of neglected hair, so it does double duty for the snakes. 'ora' is a poetic plural for a single face. Note the arrangement: Medusa's name ends one line and her face ends the next, with Perseus' own turning away wedged between them.

sentences.t:
Quantus erat, mons factus Atlas: nam barba comaeque
in silvas abeunt,
sentences.l: As great as he was, Atlas was made a mountain: for his beard and his hair go off into forests,
sentences.i: Atlas became a mountain, as big as he had been: his beard and his hair pass off into forests,
sentences.n: 'Quantus erat' is 'as big as he was': the change keeps his scale exactly, which is the point of the line and the reason a man can become a mountain. 'factus' has no 'est' beside it; the verb is simply left out, which Latin does freely. Then the tense jumps to the present ('abeunt'), and Ovid holds that present right through the transformation so that the reader watches it happen.

sentences.t:
iuga sunt umerique manusque,
quod caput ante fuit, summo est in monte cacumen,
ossa lapis fiunt:
sentences.l: his shoulders and arms are ridges; what before was head is a peak on the mountain-top; his bones become stone:
sentences.i: his shoulders and arms are ridges; what was his head before is the summit on the mountain's top; his bones turn to rock;
sentences.n: The clauses are stripped to subject, verb 'to be', and new thing, so the passage reads as a list of substitutions, one body part swapped for one piece of landscape. 'quod caput ante fuit' is a relative clause standing as the subject of its sentence, 'the thing which was his head before'. 'manus' in Latin covers the arm as well as the hand, which is why 'ridges' fits the picture better than 'hands' would.

sentences.t:
tum partes auctus in omnes
crevit in inmensum (sic, di, statuistis) et omne
cum tot sideribus caelum requievit in illo.
sentences.l: then, increased in all directions, he grew to the immeasurable - thus, gods, you ordained it - and the whole sky, with so many stars, came to rest upon him.
sentences.i: then, swollen out on every side, he grew beyond measure - so you gods decreed - and the whole sky, with all its many stars, settled to rest upon him.
sentences.n: 'auctus in omnes partes' is passive in form but reflexive in sense, 'having grown himself out in every direction'; Magnus prints 'auctus', while some editions print 'altus', 'grown tall', which narrows the growth to height alone. 'sic, di, statuistis' is an apostrophe: Ovid breaks off from telling the story to address the gods directly, and he does the same to his characters elsewhere in the poem. 'requievit' is exactly chosen: the sky rests on Atlas, and that rest is his endless labour.

sentences.t:
Clauserat Hippotades aeterno carcere ventos,
admonitorque operum caelo clarissimus alto
Lucifer ortus erat.
sentences.l: The son of Hippotes had shut the winds in their eternal prison, and the Morning Star, the reminder of work, brightest in the high sky, had risen.
sentences.i: The son of Hippotes had locked the winds in their everlasting prison, and the Morning Star, brightest in the high sky, had risen to call men to their work.
sentences.n: 'Hippotades' is Aeolus, keeper of the winds, named by patronymic as Atlas was a moment ago. Magnus prints 'aeterno carcere', 'in an eternal prison'; some editions print 'Aetnaeo', 'the prison under Etna', which names a place instead of a term. 'admonitor operum' does the work of a whole clause: the Morning Star is the thing that tells a farmer the working day has begun.

sentences.t:
Pennis ligat ille resumptis
parte ab utraque pedes teloque accingitur unco
et liquidum motis talaribus aera findit.
sentences.l: He binds his feet with the wings taken up again on either side, and girds himself with the hooked weapon, and splits the liquid air with his winged sandals set moving.
sentences.i: He straps the wings back on, one to each foot, girds on the hooked blade, and cleaves the clear air with his sandals beating.
sentences.n: 'pennis ... resumptis' and 'motis talaribus' are ablatives of means rather than ablative absolutes: he binds his feet with the wings taken up again, and splits the air with his sandals set moving, the participle doing adjectival work inside the instrument. The distinction is worth holding on to, since true absolutes are everywhere in this part as well ('positis ... templis' at 606, 'cadente die' at 627). 'telo unco' is the harpe, the curved sword with a hook that beheaded Medusa. 'liquidum aera' treats air as a clear fluid, which makes 'findit', 'splits', exact rather than metaphorical.

sentences.t:
Gentibus innumeris circumque infraque relictis
Aethiopum populos Cepheaque conspicit arva.
sentences.l: With countless nations left behind, around and below, he catches sight of the peoples of the Ethiopians and the fields of Cepheus.
sentences.i: Leaving countless nations behind him on every side and beneath him, he sights the peoples of Ethiopia and the lands of Cepheus.
sentences.n: Another ablative absolute, 'gentibus ... relictis', with the two adverbs tucked inside it. 'Aethiopes' for Greek and Roman writers meant the peoples south of Egypt. Cepheus is their king, husband of Cassiope and father of Andromeda, and 'Cephea arva' names the kingdom by an adjective made from its king's name, a very common shortcut in verse.

sentences.t:
Illic inmeritam maternae pendere linguae
Andromedan poenas iniustus iusserat Ammon.
sentences.l: There unjust Ammon had ordered Andromeda, undeserving, to pay the penalties of her mother's tongue.
sentences.i: There unjust Ammon had ordered Andromeda, who had done nothing, to pay the penalty for her mother's tongue.
sentences.n: 'Andromedan' keeps the Greek accusative ending -an, which Ovid uses for Greek names and the edition prints as it stands. 'poenas pendere' is the fixed idiom 'to pay a penalty'. 'inmeritam' comes a whole line before its noun, so the reader knows she is innocent before learning who she is, and 'iniustus' does the same for the god. Ammon is the ram-horned Libyan and Egyptian god whom the Greeks identified with Zeus; his oracle demanded the sacrifice, and the offence being paid for is the boast about beauty that Andromeda herself will report at 687 - whose beauty exactly, the Latin leaves open there.

sentences.t:
Quam simul ad duras religatam bracchia cautes
vidit Abantiades (nisi quod levis aura capillos
moverat et tepido manabant lumina fletu,
marmoreum ratus esset opus),
sentences.l: And as soon as the son of Abas saw her, bound as to her arms to the hard rocks - but that a light breeze had stirred her hair and her eyes ran with warm weeping, he would have thought her a work of marble -
sentences.i: And the moment Perseus saw her, her arms chained to the hard rock - had a light breeze not stirred her hair and warm tears not run from her eyes, he would have taken her for a work of marble -
sentences.n: 'religatam bracchia' is the Greek accusative of respect: she is bound 'as to her arms', with the accusative naming the part affected. Latin took the construction from Greek and uses it constantly with participles of binding, wounding and clothing - 'veiled as to her head', 'pierced as to his side'. 'Quam' is a connecting relative opening the sentence, 'and her'. The parenthesis is an unreal condition ('ratus esset', he would have thought), and the only two things separating her from a statue are moving hair and running tears: the comparison to sculpture is exact, since she is fixed in place and looked at.

sentences.t:
trahit inscius ignes
et stupet et visae correptus imagine formae
paene suas quatere est oblitus in aere pennas.
sentences.l: he draws in fires without knowing it, and is stunned, and, seized by the image of the beauty he has seen, almost forgot to beat his wings in the air.
sentences.i: he takes fire without knowing it, and stands stunned; caught by the sight of the beauty before him, he all but forgot to beat his wings.
sentences.n: 'trahit ignes', 'draws in fires', is the ordinary Latin way of saying a man falls in love, the fire taken in like breath. 'inscius' is a nominative adjective describing him where English would use an adverb, 'unwittingly': Latin habitually puts on the person what English puts on the verb. 'oblitus est' takes the infinitive 'quatere', 'forgot to shake'. The tense slides mid-sentence from present (trahit, stupet) to perfect (oblitus est) - Ovid speeds up and then lands on the moment.

sentences.t:
Ut stetit, “o” dixit “non istis digna catenis,
sed quibus inter se cupidi iunguntur amantes,
sentences.l: When he had halted, 'O you,' he said, 'not deserving these chains, but those with which longing lovers are joined to one another,
sentences.i: Once he had come to a stop, he said: 'You who deserve not these chains, but the chains that desiring lovers are bound with, each to each,
sentences.n: 'digna' takes an ablative of the thing deserved (catenis), and the whole sentence turns on that one case, since the same ablative carries both the iron chains she is in and the metaphorical chains of love he offers - the compliment and the presumption are the same grammatical stroke. 'istis' is the demonstrative of the second person, 'those chains of yours there'; it often carries a sneer, though here it merely points.

sentences.t:
pande requirenti nomen terraeque tuumque,
et cur vincla geras.”
sentences.l: disclose to one who asks the name both of your land and your own, and why you wear bonds.'
sentences.i: tell one who asks the name of your country and your own name, and why you are in chains.'
sentences.n: 'requirenti' is another participle standing as a noun, here in the dative, 'to [me] asking': Perseus does not say 'me'. The doubled '-que ... -que' in 'terraeque tuumque' is the epic 'both ... and', a mannerism of high verse. 'cur ... geras' is subjunctive because it is an indirect question depending on 'pande'.

sentences.t:
Primo silet illa, nec audet
adpellare virum virgo; manibusque modestos
celasset vultus, si non religata fuisset:
sentences.l: At first she is silent, and the maiden does not dare to address the man; and she would have hidden her modest face with her hands, if she had not been bound:
sentences.i: At first she says nothing: a girl, she does not dare speak to a man; and she would have hidden her modest face in her hands, had she not been tied.
sentences.n: 'adpellare virum virgo' sets the two nouns side by side so that they touch, man and unmarried girl, and the whole reason for her silence lies in that juxtaposition. 'celasset' is syncopated for 'celavisset' - a second unreal condition in a few lines, and this one makes her chains the reason her face can be seen at all. The edition prints 'adpellare' where later texts print 'appellare'; we keep the edition's spelling.

sentences.t: lumina, quod potuit, lacrimis inplevit obortis.
sentences.l: her eyes - the thing she could do - she filled with tears that rose up.
sentences.i: What she could do, she did: she filled her eyes with welling tears.
sentences.n: 'quod potuit' is a parenthetic relative, 'the [one thing] which she was able [to do]' - three words that carry the whole pathos of the moment, dropped into the middle of the line without comment. 'obortis' is 'having risen up', used of tears coming to the surface. 'lumina', literally 'lights', is standard poetic usage for eyes.

sentences.t:
Saepius instanti, sua ne delicta fateri
nolle videretur, nomen terraeque suumque,
quantaque maternae fuerit fiducia formae,
indicat.
sentences.l: To him pressing her more and more - so that she should not seem unwilling to confess offences of her own - the name of her land and her own, and how great the confidence in her mother's beauty had been, she tells.
sentences.i: As he pressed her again and again, she told him - so as not to seem unwilling to confess to faults of her own - the name of her country and her own name, and how great her mother's confidence in her beauty had been.
sentences.n: The main verb 'indicat' is held back to the first word of the fourth line, after everything it governs; making the reader wait for the verb is a hexameter habit worth expecting rather than resisting. 'instanti' is a participle as a noun in the dative, 'to him pressing'. 'ne ... videretur' is a negative purpose clause. 'maternae ... formae' is an adjective doing the work of a genitive, 'of her mother's beauty' - the confidence and the beauty are both Cassiope's, though the Latin could be read as confidence in a beauty inherited from her. Her fear is that silence would look like guilt about something she had done herself, when the fault was entirely her mother's.

sentences.t:
Et nondum memoratis omnibus unda
insonuit, veniensque inmenso belua ponto
inminet et latum sub pectore possidet aequor.
sentences.l: And with not yet everything recounted, the water roared, and a beast coming over the immense sea looms near, and takes possession of the broad water beneath its breast.
sentences.i: And before she had told it all, the water roared, and a monster came on over the vast sea, looming near, covering the wide surface with its breast.
sentences.n: 'nondum memoratis omnibus' is an ablative absolute with the negative inside it, 'everything not yet having been told', where English wants 'before she had finished'. The tenses lurch: the perfect 'insonuit' for the one sudden noise, then the presents 'inminet' and 'possidet' to hold the creature there above them. 'possidet aequor' is the verb of owning property: its sheer size is rendered as possession.

sentences.t:
Conclamat virgo: genitor lugubris et una
mater adest, ambo miseri, sed iustius illa.
sentences.l: The maiden cries out: her mourning father and, together with him, her mother is there, both wretched, but she more justly.
sentences.i: The girl screams. Her father is there in his grief and her mother with him, both of them wretched - but she with better cause.
sentences.n: 'sed iustius illa' is three words of judgement dropped in without explanation: the mother's misery is 'more just' because the boast that brought this on the daughter was hers. Ovid does not spell it out and does not need to. 'adest' is singular although it has two subjects, agreeing with the nearer one, which is normal Latin. 'una' here is the adverb 'together with', not the numeral.

sentences.t:
Nec secum auxilium, sed dignos tempore fletus
plangoremque ferunt vinctoque in corpore adhaerent,
cum sic hospes ait:
sentences.l: And they bring no help with them, but weeping worthy of the moment, and beating of the breast, and they cling to the bound body, when the stranger speaks thus:
sentences.i: They bring no help with them, only weeping to match the hour, and beating of the breast, and they cling to her chained body - when the stranger says:
sentences.n: 'dignos tempore' quietly measures how useless the tears are: they are 'worthy of the occasion' and are all the occasion is given. 'plangor' is the loud ritual beating of breast and arms performed at a death, so the parents are already mourning her as dead. 'vincto in corpore' is 'on the bound body', not 'on her': she has become an object to be wept over. 'cum ... ait' is the inverted cum-clause, in which the 'when' clause carries the new event; English does the same thing with a dash.

sentences.t:
“Lacrimarum longa manere
tempora vos poterunt: ad opem brevis hora ferendam est.
sentences.l: 'Long times of tears will be able to await you: for help to be brought there is a short hour.
sentences.i: 'There will be long time enough for tears; the hour for bringing help is short.
sentences.n: 'ad opem ferendam' is a gerundive of purpose, 'for help to be brought', that is, 'for bringing help' - the standard Latin way of expressing purpose around a noun, and worth learning to read straight through. 'manere' takes the accusative of the person waited for ('vos'). The line is built as a balance: long times against a short hour, tears against action.

sentences.t:
Hanc ego si peterem Perseus Iove natus et illa,
quam clausam inplevit fecundo Iuppiter auro,
sentences.l: If I were seeking her, I, Perseus, born of Jupiter and of her whom, shut away, Jupiter filled with fruitful gold,
sentences.i: If I were asking for her hand - I, Perseus, son of Jupiter and of the woman Jupiter filled with fruitful gold in her locked chamber -
sentences.n: 'peterem' is imperfect subjunctive, opening an unreal condition ('if I were suing for her') which he will then make real by the end of the speech. 'Hanc' is 'this girl': she is spoken of in the third person, chained, while she listens. 'clausam inplevit' compresses the assault into two words - Danae was shut in by her own father, and the participle makes her confinement the very condition of the act. See this part's advisory.

sentences.t:
Gorgonis anguicomae Perseus superator et alis
aerias ausus iactatis ire per auras,
praeferrer cunctis certe gener.
sentences.l: Perseus, the vanquisher of the snake-haired Gorgon, and the man who dared go through the airy breezes on beaten wings - I would surely be preferred to all as a son-in-law.
sentences.i: Perseus, conqueror of the snake-haired Gorgon, the man who dared travel the high winds on beating wings - surely I would be chosen before all others as your son-in-law.
sentences.n: The main verb 'praeferrer' waits until the fourth line of the sentence, after the whole résumé has been recited: the delay is itself the boast. 'anguicomae' is a compound of the kind Ovid coins freely, literally 'snake-haired'. 'alis ... iactatis' is an ablative of means with 'ire', 'to go on wings beaten', not an absolute - the wings are what he travels on. He gives his own name twice within three lines, which is not an accident of composition.

sentences.t:
Addere tantis
dotibus et meritum, faveant modo numina, tempto:
ut mea sit servata mea virtute, paciscor.”
sentences.l: To such great endowments I am trying to add a service too - let the divine powers only favour me - I bargain that she, saved by my courage, be mine.'
sentences.i: To such advantages I am trying to add a service as well - only let the gods be with me. These are my terms: saved by my courage, let her be mine.'
sentences.n: 'dotes' are the gifts a man brings - birth, deeds - set against the dowry a bride brings, which is the same word; he is turning his pedigree into a marriage settlement, and the next sentence will complete the transaction. 'faveant modo numina' is a wish in the subjunctive dropped in as a parenthesis. 'ut ... sit ... paciscor' is 'I strike a bargain that she be mine', and the doubled 'mea ... mea' presses the claim twice inside one clause.

sentences.t:
Accipiunt legem (quis enim dubitaret?) et orant
promittuntque super regnum dotale parentes.
sentences.l: The parents accept the terms - for who would hesitate? - and beg, and promise besides the kingdom as a dowry.
sentences.i: Her parents accept the terms - who would hesitate? - and beg him to act, and promise the kingdom as her dowry into the bargain.
sentences.n: 'legem' is the term of a contract, keeping up the language of the bargain from the line before. 'dubitaret' is subjunctive in a rhetorical question, 'who would hesitate?', and the aside is Ovid's own, not the parents'. 'super' here is the adverb 'over and above', not the preposition - a small trap worth watching for. The kingdom offered as 'dotale' completes the joke: he asked for a dowry-marriage and they raise the price themselves.

sentences.t:
Ecce velut navis praefixo concita rostro
sulcat aquas, iuvenum sudantibus acta lacertis,
sentences.l: See: as a ship, driven on with its beak fixed in front, furrows the waters, urged by the sweating arms of young men,
sentences.i: And now - as a ship with its ram set at the prow furrows the water, driven by the sweating arms of young men,
sentences.n: A simile begins here and runs to 710, with 'velut' ('as') answered by 'sic' ('so') at 708: the long two-limbed simile is a fixture of epic, and it pays to read the whole shape before working out the sense of any part. 'rostrum' is the beak or ram of a warship, the same word as a bird's beak. 'sulcat' is the ploughing verb: the ship cuts a furrow in the sea.

sentences.t:
sic fera dimotis inpulsu pectoris undis
tantum aberat scopulis, quantum Balearica torto
funda potest plumbo medii transmittere caeli:
sentences.l: so the beast, with the waves pushed apart by the drive of its breast, was as far from the rocks as a Balearic sling can send whirled lead across the middle of the sky:
sentences.i: so the creature came on, shouldering the waves apart, and was as far from the rocks as a Balearic sling can send its whirling shot through the open air.
sentences.n: 'dimotis undis' is another ablative absolute, 'the waves having been pushed aside'. 'medii ... caeli' is a partitive genitive picked up by 'tantum ... quantum': 'as much of the middle air as'. The Balearic islanders were famous slingers, hired as auxiliaries by Carthage and then by Rome, and their range is used here as a plain unit of distance - the epic simile drops for a moment into military measurement.

sentences.t:
cum subito iuvenis pedibus tellure repulsa
arduus in nubes abiit.
sentences.l: when suddenly the young man, the earth thrust back by his feet, went off steeply into the clouds.
sentences.i: when suddenly the young man pushed off from the ground and shot up steeply into the clouds.
sentences.n: 'tellure repulsa' is an ablative absolute carrying the main physical action: 'the earth having been pushed back by his feet' is how Latin says 'he kicked off'. 'arduus' is an adjective describing him, not an adverb describing the going - 'he went, steep' - and Latin regularly puts on the subject what English puts on the verb.

sentences.t:
Ut in aequore summo
umbra viri visa est, visa fera saevit in umbra.
sentences.l: When on the surface of the water the shadow of the man was seen, the beast rages upon the shadow it has seen.
sentences.i: When the man's shadow showed on the surface of the sea, the beast raged at the shadow it saw.
sentences.n: 'visa est ... visa' repeats the participle across the line, and the line begins and ends on 'umbra': the shadow is the whole content of the verse, as it is the whole of what the monster attacks. Magnus prints the ablative 'visa ... in umbra', 'upon the shadow it has seen'; some editions print the accusative 'visam ... in umbram', which makes it 'rages against the shadow', the ordinary construction for attacking something. The picture is the same either way; the grammar is not.

sentences.t:
Utque Iovis praepes, vacuo cum vidit in arvo
praebentem Phoebo liventia terga draconem,
occupat aversum, neu saeva retorqueat ora,
squamigeris avidos figit cervicibus ungues,
sentences.l: And as the swift bird of Jupiter, when it has seen in an empty field a snake offering its blue-black back to the sun, seizes it from behind, and, so that it may not twist round its savage jaws, fixes its greedy talons in the scaly neck,
sentences.i: And as Jupiter's bird, spotting a snake in an open field with its livid back turned up to the sun, takes it from behind and - so it cannot swing its cruel jaws round - sinks its greedy talons into the scaled neck,
sentences.n: A second simile, again 'ut ... sic'. 'Iovis praepes' is the eagle, named by function ('Jupiter's swift-flier') rather than by name, as Ovid prefers. 'aversum' is a participle standing for a noun, 'him turned away', and it carries the whole tactic in one word. 'neu' introduces a negative purpose clause. 'squamigeris', 'scale-bearing', is one more of the built compounds this poem likes; 'Phoebo' is the sun-god's name standing in for the sunlight.

sentences.t:
sic celeri missus praeceps per inane volatu
terga ferae pressit dextroque frementis in armo
Inachides ferrum curvo tenus abdidit hamo.
sentences.l: so the descendant of Inachus, launched headlong through the void in swift flight, pressed the beast's back and, in the right shoulder of the roaring creature, buried his blade as far as the curved hook.
sentences.i: so Perseus, flung headlong through the empty air in swift flight, came down on the creature's back and drove his blade into the right shoulder of the roaring beast, up to the curved hook.
sentences.n: 'Inachides' is 'descendant of Inachus', the river-god founder of Argos: a third name for Perseus in this part, after Abantiades and Perseus itself, and the poem expects the reader to keep up. 'tenus' is a postposition and follows its ablative ('curvo ... hamo'), 'as far as the hook'. 'frementis' is a genitive participle standing alone for the roaring beast. 'inane', 'the void', is the neuter adjective used as a noun once again.

sentences.t:
Vulnere laesa gravi modo se sublimis in auras
attollit, modo subdit aquis, modo more ferocis
versat apri, quem turba canum circumsona terret.
sentences.l: Hurt by the heavy wound, now it lifts itself high into the air, now puts itself under the water, now turns as a fierce boar does whom a crowd of hounds baying all round terrifies.
sentences.i: Wounded deep, it now heaves itself high into the air, now dives under the water, now wheels like a wild boar with a pack of hounds baying all round it.
sentences.n: 'modo ... modo ... modo', 'now ... now ... now', gives three moves in three clauses, and the rhythm of the line does the thrashing. The 'se' of the first clause serves the other two as well - 'subdit [se] aquis', 'versat [se]' - a carrying-over of one word across several clauses that Latin does freely and English cannot. 'circumsona' is a compound, 'sounding round about'; it is the surrounding noise that maddens the boar, and the simile carries that maddening across to a creature underwater.

sentences.t: Ille avidos morsus velocibus effugit alis
sentences.l: He escapes the greedy bites on swift wings
sentences.n: 'Ille' switches the subject back to Perseus without naming him: Latin runs a two-party fight on demonstratives alone, and keeping track of who is 'ille' and who 'illa' is much of the work of reading a battle scene. 'morsus' is a plural of the act of biting rather than of the wound.

sentences.t:
quaque patet, nunc terga cavis super obsita conchis,
nunc laterum costas, nunc qua tenuissima cauda
desinit in piscem, falcato vulnerat ense.
sentences.l: and wherever it lies open - now the back above, thick-set with hollow shells, now the ribs of the flanks, now where the tail at its thinnest ends in a fish - he wounds it with his hooked sword.
sentences.i: and wherever it lay open - now the back above, crusted with hollow shells, now the ribs of the flanks, now where the tail tapers away into a fish - he cut it with his hooked sword.
sentences.n: 'quaque patet' is 'and where[ever] it is open', an adverbial relative with no antecedent, which English fills out with 'wherever'. The three 'nunc' clauses are all objects of a single verb held to the very end of the sentence, so three targets are named before the reader is told what is done to them. Magnus prints 'vulnerat', 'wounds'; some editions print 'verberat', 'lashes at', which turns cutting into beating. 'desinit in piscem' - the body ends in a fish's tail, the standard shape of a sea-monster in ancient art.

sentences.t:
Belua puniceo mixtos cum sanguine fluctus
ore vomit: maduere graves adspergine pennae.
sentences.l: The beast vomits from its mouth waves mixed with crimson blood: the wings grew heavy, soaked with the spray.
sentences.i: The monster spews from its mouth water mixed with crimson blood; the wings grew heavy, drenched with the spray.
sentences.n: 'maduere' is 'maduerunt', the -ere perfect again - no longer worth flagging, only noticing. 'graves' is predicative: the wings became heavy by becoming wet, so one adjective carries the whole consequence of the line before. 'puniceus' is the red of Phoenician purple-dye, an expensive colour used here of blood. The edition prints 'adspergine' where later texts write 'aspergine'; we keep the edition's spelling.

sentences.t:
Nec bibulis ultra Perseus talaribus ausus
credere, conspexit scopulum, qui vertice summo
stantibus exstat aquis, operitur ab aequore moto.
sentences.l: And Perseus, not daring to trust his soaking sandals any further, caught sight of a rock which stands out at its topmost point when the waters are still, and is covered over by the sea when it is stirred.
sentences.i: Perseus, not daring to trust his sodden sandals any longer, caught sight of a rock whose top stands clear when the water is still and is covered when the sea runs.
sentences.n: 'bibulis' means 'drinking', used of things that soak liquid up: the sandals are drinking the spray, which is why they no longer hold him. 'stantibus aquis' and 'ab aequore moto' are a matched pair, ablative absolute against ablative of agent, still water on one side of the rock and moving water on the other. Note the two present tenses: they describe what the rock always does, so the sentence steps out of the fight for a moment to say what kind of rock it is.

sentences.t:
Nixus eo rupisque tenens iuga prima sinistra
ter quater exegit repetita per ilia ferrum.
sentences.l: Braced on it, and holding the crag's first ridges with his left, three times, four times he drove the blade through the flanks struck again and again.
sentences.i: Braced on it, gripping the crag's first ledge with his left hand, three and four times he drove his blade through the beast's guts.
sentences.n: 'ter quater', 'three times, four times', is an epic formula for an indefinite many; the two numerals stand together without a connective. 'repetita' agrees with 'ilia' and means 'attacked again and again' - 'repetere' is the word for coming back at a target - so the participle puts the repetition on the wound rather than on the sword. 'sinistra' is 'his left', with 'manu' left out, exactly as English says 'his left'.

sentences.t:
Litora cum plausu clamor superasque deorum
inplevere domos:
sentences.l: Shouting, with applause, filled the shores and the high houses of the gods:
sentences.i: The shore rang with shouting and applause, and the noise filled the high halls of the gods as well:
sentences.n: The verb is plural ('inplevere' = 'inpleverunt') although the only nominative is singular ('clamor'): the ablative phrase 'cum plausu' is felt as a second subject, so shouting and clapping together do the filling - agreement by sense rather than by grammar. 'superas ... domos' are the houses above, that is, heaven, and the noise crosses from earth to sky inside a single line.

sentences.t:
gaudent generumque salutant
auxiliumque domus servatoremque fatentur
Cassiope Cepheusque pater.
sentences.l: they rejoice, and greet him as son-in-law, and acknowledge him the help and the saviour of the house - Cassiope and Cepheus the father.
sentences.i: Cassiope and Cepheus the father rejoice, hail him as their son-in-law, and own him the help and the saviour of their house.
sentences.n: The three verbs come first and the subjects last: the names arrive only after the whole reaction has been described, a standard hexameter shape that is always worth waiting out rather than reordering too soon. 'generum salutare' is to greet someone as son-in-law, and the verb does the work of a public ceremony - the betrothal is made by saying it. 'Cepheus pater' is 'Cepheus the father', naming his role, not a title.

sentences.t:
Resoluta catenis
incedit virgo, pretiumque et causa laboris.
sentences.l: Loosed from her chains the maiden walks forward, both the prize and the cause of the labour.
sentences.i: Freed from her chains the girl walks forward, at once the prize of the exploit and its cause.
sentences.n: 'incedit' is the verb of a stately walk, used of goddesses and queens: the first thing she does unbound is to move with dignity. 'resoluta catenis' is an ablative of separation with no preposition, 'loosed from chains'. 'pretium et causa' stands in apposition to 'virgo' with no verb of its own, and the two nouns are the sting of the line: she is both what the work was for and what made it necessary.

sentences.t: Ipse manus hausta victrices abluit unda,
sentences.l: He himself washes his conquering hands with water drawn up,
sentences.n: 'hausta ... unda' is an ablative of means wrapped around the middle of the line, 'with water drawn up' - the water is what he washes with, not a detached absolute clause - and the word order holds 'manus' apart from its adjective 'victrices' so that the adjective lands last. Washing after a killing is not fastidiousness: spilled blood is pollution, and it is cleaned off before the sacred object is handled.

sentences.t:
anguiferumque caput dura ne laedat harena,
mollit humum foliis natasque sub aequore virgas
sternit et inponit Phorcynidos ora Medusae.
sentences.l: and, so that the hard sand may not damage the snake-bearing head, he softens the ground with leaves, and spreads out shoots grown under the water, and lays upon them the face of Medusa, daughter of Phorcys.
sentences.i: and, so that the hard sand should not damage the snake-bearing head, he softened the ground with leaves, spread out shoots grown under the sea, and laid on them the face of Medusa, Phorcys' daughter.
sentences.n: The purpose clause ('ne ... laedat') comes before the action it explains, so the care is stated before the thing done. 'anguiferum' is another built compound, 'snake-carrying'. 'Phorcynidos' is a Greek genitive in -idos, kept as the edition prints it: Medusa is the daughter of the sea-god Phorcys, which is why her line belongs to the sea - and why what happens next happens in the water.

sentences.t:
Virga recens bibulaque etiamnum viva medulla
vim rapuit monstri tactuque induruit huius
percepitque novum ramis et fronde rigorem.
sentences.l: The shoot, fresh and still living with its thirsty pith, seized the power of the monster, and hardened at its touch, and took on a new stiffness in its branches and its leaf.
sentences.i: The shoot, still fresh and alive with its thirsty pith, took in the monster's power, hardened at its touch, and received a new stiffness through branch and leaf.
sentences.n: 'monstrum' here is Medusa's head, called a monster as the source of the power rather than as a creature. 'vim rapuit' is 'snatched the force', an unusually active verb for a plant, and it makes the shoot the agent of its own petrifaction rather than the victim. 'bibula ... medulla' is an ablative of description, 'with its absorbent pith', which is precisely why the power soaks in. 'rigor' means both stiffness and cold, and carries the change from living wood to stone in one word.

sentences.t:
At pelagi nymphae factum mirabile temptant
pluribus in virgis et idem contingere gaudent
seminaque ex illis iterant iactata per undas.
sentences.l: But the nymphs of the sea try the marvellous happening on more shoots, and rejoice that the same thing comes about, and repeat the seeds from them, flung through the waves.
sentences.i: But the sea-nymphs tried the marvel on more shoots, delighted that the same thing happened each time, and sowed the seed from them again and again, flinging it through the waves.
sentences.n: 'temptant' means 'test, try out': the nymphs run an experiment, repeating it to see whether it holds - a strikingly cool word to use of a miracle, and typical of the way this poem treats its own wonders. 'contingere' is an infinitive in indirect statement after 'gaudent', 'rejoice that it turns out'. 'semina ... iterant', 'they repeat the seeds', is compressed for 'they sow them over and over', and 'iactata' is a participle where English wants a second verb.

sentences.t:
Nunc quoque curaliis eadem natura remansit,
duritiam tacto capiant ut ab aere, quodque
vimen in aequore erat, fiat super aequora saxum.
sentences.l: Now too the same nature has remained in corals, so that they take hardness from the air once touched, and what was a pliant twig in the sea becomes stone above the sea.
sentences.i: Even now the same nature has stayed in coral: it takes on hardness from the air the moment it is touched by it, and what was a pliant shoot in the water turns to stone above the water.
sentences.n: 'quoque' here is the plain adverb 'too', and its pairing with 'Nunc' settles it - but the word is a standing trap in this poem, where it is often 'quo-que', 'and with which'. The edition spells the word 'curaliis' for 'coralliis' and we keep it. 'ut' is postponed inside its own clause ('duritiam ... capiant ut'), a licence verse takes freely. Ancient natural history held that coral is soft underwater and hardens on contact with air, so the tale ends where all Ovid's aetiologies aim: at a thing the reader can pick up and hold. Note 'aequore ... aequora' repeated for under the water and over it, closing the passage on the word it turns on.
